items.title: $50,000 in These 3 Pipeline Dividend Stocks Could Pay You $1,900 a Year
items.summary: Three pipeline giants collect tolls whether gas prices soar or crater, and each carries a hidden weak spot, from leverage to commodity swings to a dividend cut in its past. Which one pays the most, and which one worries us?

items.title: Energy Transfer Just Sent a Message to Anyone Collecting $13,700 a Year by Raising Its Payout After an Earnings Miss
items.summary: Energy Transfer will pay $0.3425 a unit on November 19, its 20th straight quarterly raise, in the same quarter its earnings per unit missed Wall Street by about 20%. For a 74-year-old holding 10,000 units in a taxable account, that is $13,700 a year at a 7.1% yield. Here is why the cash covers it twice over, what the K-1 does to his tax bill and his cost basis, why the IRA is the wrong account for it, and what a swap to a 1099 pipeline would cost.

items.title: A 70-Year-Old With $1,000,000 in Hormel, AT&T and ONEOK Collects $4,230 a Month in Dividends. How Safe Is Each Check?
items.summary: Key TakeawaysA hypothetical $1,000,000 split evenly across Hormel Foods, AT&T and ONEOK pays $50,759 a year in dividends, or $4,269 a month. ONEOK’s check looks safe and growing, AT&T’s looks safe but flat, and Hormel’s looks stretched.

items.title: Why Kinder Morgan's Chairman Just Bought $15 Million in Stock
items.summary: Richard Kinder bought $15 million in KMI shares after Kinder Morgan's backlog hit a record $14.4 billion, driven by natural gas deals tied to AI data centers and utilities.

items.title: National Fuel Gas Has Paid a Dividend for 124 Straight Years. Can It Keep Going?
items.summary: National Fuel is preparing to break into two companies, and management has not said a word about what happens to the payout afterward. Income investors face a quiet risk that could keep the record alive while shrinking the check.

items.title: How Much Does a 60-Year-Old Need Invested to Replace a $125,000 Salary With Dividends and Never Sell a Share?
items.summary: One rule, never sell a share, sounds bulletproof until you check what happened to these six high-yield holdings this year. One dividend was slashed, another switched its payment schedule, and a few funds shrank even as they kept paying.
